Got it — planning recovery. Quick step-by-step we can work through together; tell me when you want to stop or focus more on any step.

1) Pick a time window. How much time can you realistically set aside in the next 24–48 hours? (10–20 minutes, 30–60 minutes, a few hours, or an evening?)

4) Plan the immediate steps to make it happen: where, what you need, and one barrier you might hit (e.g., “I’ll keep scrolling” or “I might feel guilty”). Name the barrier and a simple workaround.

5) Commit and schedule: set a start time or a trigger (e.g., “after I finish this message” or “at 8:30 PM”). Do you want me to set a quick reminder phrase you can use?

6) Follow-up: after you do it, tell me how it went in one sentence and we’ll adjust the next recovery slot.

Okay — planning recovery. I’ll walk you through a short, practical plan you can pick from and adapt. Answer any quick questions as we go (time available, how sleepy you are, and whether you’re alone or with others).

1) Check basics (2–10 minutes)
- Rate your immediate needs: hunger, thirst, bathroom, meds, sleepiness.

2) Two-hour priority: restore core energy
Pick one of these based on what you want and how tired you are:
- Short nap (20–90 minutes): 20–30 min for a quick refresh; 90 min if you can get full REM cycle. Set an alarm and a calm, dark space.  
- Gentle rest routine: 30–60 minutes of low-effort comfort — warm drink, knees-to-chest on couch, soft music or a favorite show for background.  
- Low-effort movement: 15–30 minute slow walk outside or gentle stretching if you think movement helps.

3) Evening wind-down (next 1–3 hours)
- Dim lights/screens 60–90 minutes before bed.  
- Do one calming activity: reading, a warm shower, light journaling (3 lines: what went okay today, what you’ll let go, one small thing for tomorrow).  
- Avoid heavy work, caffeine, or stressful tasks.

- Choose 1 small actionable thing to set up for tomorrow (e.g., lay out clothes, pick 2 priorities, set an easy alarm). Make it specific and tiny so it’s doable when you’re low energy.

5) If flat mood persists
- Plan one social or pleasant thing within 48 hours: a short call, coffee, or a hobby session. Not mandatory — just a gentle nudge to reconnect.

Okay — quick calming script (5–7 minutes). Do this where you won’t be disturbed.

1) Sit comfortably, feet on the floor. Close your eyes if that feels okay.  
2) Take three slow belly breaths: inhale 4 seconds, hold 4, exhale 6. Put one hand on your belly to feel it rise.  
3) Do a 60-second grounding scan: name silently five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell (or imagine), one thing you can taste.  
4) Progressive release for 90 seconds: clench your fists and tighten your shoulders for 5 seconds, then fully release; tense your jaw for 5 seconds, release; finally soften your whole face and let your shoulders drop.  
5) Finish with one slow, full breath and open your eyes. Take a sip of water.

- Full rest day: sleep in, no plans, low light, naps, gentle food — for when you need to recover energy.

- Low-stim digital detox: set specific phone-free windows (e.g., morning and evening) and replace them with reading, puzzles, or a hobby.
- Social recharge: low-pressure time with one close friend or family (coffee, easy meal, park) — good if company helps.
- Creative/flow hour(s): block 1–3 hours for something absorbing (drawing, cooking a new recipe, music, writing) to shift focus.

- Structured “do less” day: pick 1 must-do and set three “not-to-do” rules (no email, no chores, no news).  
- Pamper session at home: longer bath, face mask, good playlist/podcast, favorite snack — minimal planning, high comfort.  
- Mental reset: 30–60 min journaling prompt set (what drained me, what helped, one small next step) — clears mental clutter.
